analysis.one_liner: Expands federal heating and cooling aid to far more low-income households and protects them from shutoffs.
analysis.headline: The Heating and Cooling Relief Act never received a committee vote or floor vote in the 118th Congress, sitting with the Senate health committee for nearly two years.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would reauthorize and dramatically expand the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), the federal program that helps low-income households pay home heating and cooling bills. It raises the income cutoff for eligibility, adds a new test for any household spending 3% or more of its income on energy, authorizes $400 billion over ten years, adds dedicated cooling aid for heat waves, and requires utilities that receive program funds to refund late fees and not shut off service to assisted households for a year. It also funds grants to help high-usage households weatherize and move off fossil-fuel appliances.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income households that struggle with home energy bills. Today the program reaches a small share of eligible families: the bill's own findings cite that in 2019 only 16% of income-eligible households received assistance [S3]. The bill would roughly raise the income cutoff from 150% of the poverty line to 250% (or 80% of state median income), add eligibility for any household with a 3% or higher monthly energy burden, let applicants self-attest eligibility without proof of income or citizenship paperwork, and keep states from excluding households over a member's citizenship status [S2] [S3]. It also protects assisted households from shutoffs and late fees [S2] [S3], adds automatic heating or cooling aid in federally declared disasters and extreme heat [S3], and directs $1 billion a year to state grants for cutting high household energy burdens [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income households with high energy bills

how_it_helps.text: Expands LIHEAP eligibility to households up to 250% of the poverty line, 80% of state median income, or any household with a 3% or greater monthly energy burden, and allows self-attestation of income, citizenship, and need without documentation.
Authorizes $400 billion for the main program over fiscal years 2024-2033, plus $1 billion a year each for heat-wave cooling aid and 'just transition' grants to reduce high household energy burdens.

Bars home energy suppliers that receive program funds from charging late fees to assisted households for a year around payment (and requires refunds of fees already charged) and from shutting off service to a household for one year after it receives assistance.

Requires states to provide additional assistance for home energy arrears, raises the share of funds usable for weatherization from 15% to 25%, and requires year-round program operation, online applications, and outreach through schools and medical-equipment users.
Adds automatic cooling or heating assistance for households in areas declared major disasters or emergencies, including extreme heat and cold, without requiring proof of a medical need for cooling.

analysis.who_pays: General taxpayers fund the $400 billion authorization (about $40 billion a year versus roughly $4 billion in recent annual funding), and home energy suppliers bear the new conditions: late-fee refunds and losses, shutoff restrictions during the year after a household is assisted, data sharing with states, and notices directing late-paying households to apply for aid [S3]. The bill pushes weatherization and appliance priorities toward replacing fossil-fuel heating with electric heat pumps and community solar, which shifts demand away from fuel-oil and gas suppliers over time [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The $400 billion figure is an authorization, not an actual appropriation; Congress still has to pass separate spending each year, and nothing in this bill by itself delivers the money.

The tax cost is very large by the standards of a single program, and the paperwork-light self-attestation eligibility rules could open the program to households that would not qualify under documented income checks.

The mandate to promote reduction of fossil-fuel energy and prioritize electric heating upgrades could raise program costs per household and disadvantage regions, especially the Northeast, where delivered heating oil remains common.
Requiring utilities to absorb late-fee losses and offering percentage-of-income payment plans could add compliance costs that suppliers argue get built into rates for other customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill directly targets a real and large problem: the bill's findings cite Census survey data that about 51% of families earning under $35,000 a year cut back on medicine or food at least one month a year to pay energy bills, and that loss of energy service is a leading path into homelessness [S3]. The cost is a major expansion of federal spending (about $40 billion a year authorized) plus real compliance burdens on utilities. The main design weaknesses are that the funding must be appropriated separately each year and the self-attestation rules trade program integrity for enrollment speed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up for the rest of the Congress, so it died without any vote.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Markey introduced the bill with six Democratic and independent colleagues on February 14, 2023.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate HELP Committee the same day; no hearing, markup, or further action followed during the 118th Congress.
No roll-call vote ever occurred on the bill in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Home energy suppliers avoided the bill's late-fee refunds, shutoff restrictions, and data-sharing conditions, and taxpayers avoided the ~$40 billion-a-year authorization; low-income households with high energy bills gained nothing, and the status quo left only about 16% of eligible households served in the program's most recent cited year.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Home energy suppliers and the status quo

for.name: Edward J. Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Heating and Cooling Relief Act in the Senate.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren, Kirsten Gillibrand, Richard Blumenthal, Cory Booker, Bernie Sanders, and Alex Padilla
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction; none was a Republican.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled it for a hearing or markup during the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so the chamber's party split was never tested; all seven sponsors were Democrats or independents and no Republican cosponsored.

industries.industry: Electric and gas utilities and home energy suppliers
industries.note: The bill routes expanded federal aid to households through energy suppliers, who are paid for assisted households, and gives them new customers in arrears relief; but it also strips late fees and shutoffs from assisted households, requires data sharing, and conditions payment on outreach and payment plans. On net, suppliers keep a revenue stream while losing fee income and some collection leverage.

industries.industry: Weatherization, retrofit, and heat-pump installation contractors
industries.note: The bill raises the weatherization set-aside from 15% to 25% of program funds, prioritizes replacing fossil-fuel appliances with efficient electric heating and cooling, and funds $1 billion a year in state grants for energy-burden reduction, creating a large new pool of federally funded home upgrade work.

industries.industry: Fuel oil and natural gas heating suppliers
industries.note: The bill directs weatherization money toward replacing fossil-fuel appliances with electric alternatives and requires energy-burden reduction plans that promote moving away from fossil fuel energy, gradually shrinking demand for delivered fuels.
The bill authorizes roughly $40 billion a year of federal spending, far above LIHEAP's recent annual funding of a few billion, funded by general revenues.
